questions.stem: A 29 year old man who is 1.96 m tall with long fingers and a previous lens dislocation has sudden, severe chest pain that tore through to his back while lifting weights. He is pale and sweaty. His pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP is 158/90 mmHg in the right arm and 124/76 mmHg in the left arm. Breath sounds are equal on both sides.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Marfan's habitus, tearing pain to the back and an arm BP difference over 20 mmHg mean aortic dissection; equal breath sounds argue against pneumothorax.

steps.x: A diagnosis question in a young man with chest pain: think about what his body habitus predisposes to.

clues: 158/90 mmHg in the right arm and 124/76 mmHg in the left arm
steps.x: Tall, long fingers, lens dislocation = **Marfan's**, the strongest risk factor. Tearing pain to the back plus a **>20 mmHg** arm difference.

elim: Pericarditis gives sharp pleuritic pain eased by sitting forward, not a 34 mmHg arm difference.
MI pain builds up and does not tear through to the back or cause unequal arm pressures.
PE gives pleuritic pain and hypoxia, not a pulse deficit between arms.
Marfan's also predisposes to pneumothorax, but breath sounds are equal.

steps.x: **B. Aortic dissection.** Marfan's + tearing pain + arm BP difference = dissection.

questions.stem: A 63 year old man has a CT aortic angiogram that confirms a dissection of the descending thoracic aorta. He smokes 10 cigarettes a day, has type 2 diabetes controlled with metformin, and has never attended for review of his blood pressure. His BMI is 31 kg/m². His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 192/108 mmHg. He has no family history of note.
questions.q: Which is the most likely underlying predisposing factor?
questions.e: Hypertension is the most common association of aortic dissection; his BP is 192/108 mmHg and has never been treated.

steps.x: Several risk factors are listed: pick the one most strongly linked with dissection.

clues: never attended for review of his blood pressure
steps.x: Untreated, very high BP in an older man with no connective tissue disease.

elim: Cholesterol drives atherosclerosis and coronary disease more than medial weakening.
Obesity is not a direct cause of aortic dissection.
Smoking is the main risk factor for abdominal aortic aneurysm, not the commonest association of dissection.
Diabetes is not a recognised major association with dissection.

steps.x: **B. Hypertension.** Hypertension is the commonest association; Marfan's is the strongest risk factor.

questions.stem: A 57 year old woman has sudden severe chest pain radiating to her back. A CT aortic angiogram shows an intimal flap beginning just above the aortic valve, extending around the arch and down into the descending thoracic aorta. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 170/94 mmHg in the right arm and 140/82 mmHg in the left arm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely classification of her condition?
questions.e: Any involvement of the ascending aorta makes it Stanford type A, whatever happens distally.

steps.x: A classification question: where does the flap start?

clues: extending around the arch and down into the descending thoracic aorta
steps.x: The flap starts in the **ascending aorta**. Extension distally does not change the type.

elim: The flap is thoracic and there is no aneurysm or retroperitoneal bleed.
A penetrating ulcer is a focal crater, not a flap running from root to descending aorta.
Type B is confined to the aorta distal to the left subclavian; this involves the ascending aorta.
An intimal flap means dissection, not a simple aneurysm.

steps.x: **C. Stanford type A aortic dissection.** Ascending aorta involved = type A = surgical emergency.

questions.stem: A 74 year old man with hypertension has sudden tearing interscapular pain. A CT aortic angiogram shows a false lumen confined to the descending thoracic aorta, starting distal to the left subclavian artery. His pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 176/98 mmHg in both arms. Heart sounds are normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge
questions.e: A type B false lumen in the descending aorta delays the femoral pulse behind the radial; radio-radial delay belongs to type A.

steps.x: A finding question: match the examination sign to the Stanford type.

clues: false lumen confined to the descending thoracic aorta
distal to the left subclavian artery
steps.x: Descending aorta only = **type B**. Equal arm pressures mean the arch branches are spared.

elim: Aortic regurgitation is a type A complication; his heart sounds are normal.
Tamponade follows type A dissection into the pericardium.
Radio-radial delay comes from type A involving the arch branches; his arm pressures are equal.
Calf swelling suggests DVT, not an arterial dissection.

steps.x: **C. Radio-femoral delay.** Type B = radio-femoral delay; type A = radio-radial delay.

questions.stem: A 66 year old man is on the vascular ward with a type B aortic dissection. Twelve hours after admission he develops severe left loin pain and has passed no urine for 6 hours despite a patent catheter. His pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 168/96 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his new symptoms?
o: Renal artery compromise by the dissection
questions.e: The dissection has propagated into the renal artery, so the kidney loses its blood supply: loin pain and anuria.

steps.x: A complication question: which branch artery explains the symptoms?

clues: passed no urine for 6 hours despite a patent catheter
steps.x: New organ symptoms during a dissection mean a **branch artery** has been compromised.

elim: There is no fever, and anuria with loin pain fits loss of renal perfusion.
His catheter is patent, so this is not retention.
Contrast nephropathy causes a slow creatinine rise, not sudden loin pain.
A stone does not cause anuria in a patient with two kidneys.

steps.x: **D. Renal artery compromise by the dissection.** Anuria + loin pain in dissection = renal artery involvement.

questions.stem: A 70 year old woman is being treated for a type B aortic dissection with IV labetalol. She develops severe central abdominal pain that is out of proportion to her examination; the abdomen is soft with mild tenderness. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm and BP 150/88 mmHg. Investigations: lactate 6.2 mmol/L (<2).
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her abdominal pain?
questions.e: Pain out of proportion to a soft abdomen with a high lactate means the dissection has compromised the mesenteric arteries.

steps.x: A complication question: which artery is the flap now affecting?

clues: out of proportion to her examination
steps.x: Severe pain, soft abdomen, rising lactate: **gut ischaemia**.

elim: Cholecystitis gives RUQ pain with Murphy's sign, not a soft abdomen with high lactate.
Pancreatitis causes epigastric pain to the back with raised amylase, not this setting.
Diverticulitis causes LIF pain and fever.
Perforation gives a rigid peritonitic abdomen.

steps.x: **D. Mesenteric ischaemia from the dissection.** Abdominal pain in dissection = mesenteric compromise.

questions.stem: A 61 year old man has sudden severe pain between his shoulder blades, followed an hour later by pain and coldness in his left leg. The leg is pale with absent femoral and foot pulses. He is in sinus rhythm. His pulse rate is 100 bpm and BP 186/100 mmHg in the right arm. A chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Interscapular pain then a pulseless leg with a widened mediastinum: the dissection has compromised the femoral circulation, causing acute limb ischaemia.

steps.x: A diagnosis question: link the chest pain to the leg.
Back pain, then **acute limb ischaemia**, in sinus rhythm, with a **widened mediastinum**.

elim: DVT gives a swollen, warm leg with pulses present.
Disc prolapse does not cause a cold, pulseless leg.
Rupture gives abdominal or back pain with shock; he is hypertensive with a widened mediastinum.
Cord compression causes weakness and sensory loss, not an absent femoral pulse.

steps.x: **A. Aortic dissection.** Chest/back pain + pulseless limb + wide mediastinum = dissection.

questions.stem: A 64 year old man has sudden tearing chest pain radiating to his back. BP is 168/92 mmHg in the right arm and 132/80 mmHg in the left arm. He has a new early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. His pulse rate is 104 bpm. ECG (see item resources).

visual.title: 12-lead ECG
visual.caption: Inferior ST elevation: the dissection has compromised the right coronary ostium.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Tearing pain, a 36 mmHg arm difference and a new AR murmur mean a type A dissection; the inferior ST elevation is coronary malperfusion.

steps.x: A diagnosis question with an ECG: do not let ST elevation make you forget the rest of the stem.

clues: tearing chest pain radiating to his back
168/92 mmHg in the right arm and 132/80 mmHg in the left arm
steps.x: The ECG shows inferior ST elevation, but the history and signs are a **dissection** involving the **aortic root**.

elim: Pericarditis gives widespread saddle ST elevation, not territorial change with an arm BP difference.
The arm difference and new AR murmur point to a dissection compromising the right coronary ostium.
PE does not cause an AR murmur or a pulse deficit.
Type B spares the aortic root, so it cannot cause AR or coronary ischaemia.

steps.x: **D. Stanford type A aortic dissection.** ST elevation + arm BP difference + AR murmur = type A dissection.

questions.stem: A 58 year old woman is in resus with a confirmed Stanford type A aortic dissection awaiting theatre. She becomes breathless and light-headed. Her pulse rate is 132 bpm and BP 82/60 mmHg. Her jugular venous pressure is raised to the angle of the jaw. Her chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most likely additional finding on examination?
o: Reduced breath sounds on the left
questions.e: Hypotension and a raised JVP in type A dissection mean cardiac tamponade (blood in the pericardium), which muffles the heart sounds.

steps.x: A finding question: name the complication first, then its sign.

clues: raised to the angle of the jaw
steps.x: Hypotension + raised JVP + clear chest = **Beck's triad** under way.

elim: Her chest is clear, so this is not pulmonary oedema.
A collapsing pulse fits chronic AR, not hypotension with a raised JVP.
Haemothorax would cause hypovolaemia with a low JVP.
Tension pneumothorax is not a complication of dissection.

steps.x: **C. Muffled heart sounds.** Type A + shock + raised JVP = tamponade = muffled heart sounds.

questions.stem: A 52 year old man is admitted with a type A aortic dissection. He becomes increasingly breathless. His pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 150/42 mmHg and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. JVP is raised. There are bibasal crackles, a third heart sound and an early diastolic murmur loudest at the left sternal edge. There is mild ankle oedema.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of his breathlessness?
questions.e: The dissection has distorted the aortic valve annulus causing acute AR, with a wide pulse pressure and cardiac failure (crackles, S3, raised JVP).

steps.x: A cause question: which complication explains a murmur and heart failure?

clues: bibasal crackles, a third heart sound
early diastolic murmur loudest at the left sternal edge
steps.x: Wide pulse pressure + early diastolic murmur = **AR**; crackles, S3, JVP = **heart failure** from it.

elim: Tamponade gives hypotension and muffled sounds, not a murmur with crackles and a wide pulse pressure.
Haemothorax gives unilateral dullness, not bibasal crackles and an S3.
There is no fever, and the S3 and murmur point to the heart.
PE would not cause an early diastolic murmur or pulmonary oedema.

steps.x: **A. Acute aortic regurgitation.** Type A + early diastolic murmur + failure = acute AR.

questions.stem: A 68 year old woman has sudden chest pain radiating to her back. Thirty minutes later she develops weakness of her left arm and leg and slurred speech. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 174/96 mmHg in the left arm and 140/80 mmHg in the right arm. A CT aortic angiogram shows a flap in the ascending aorta extending into the brachiocephalic trunk.
questions.q: Which is the most likely cause of her neurological symptoms?
o: Carotid artery compromise by the dissection
questions.e: The flap has propagated into the brachiocephalic trunk and right carotid, causing a right hemisphere stroke (left-sided weakness).

steps.x: A cause question: trace the flap into the branch artery.

clues: flap in the ascending aorta extending into the brachiocephalic trunk
weakness of her left arm and leg
steps.x: A **type A** flap entering the arch branches: neurological complaints are a recognised type A complication.

elim: Encephalopathy causes headache and confusion, not a focal hemiparesis.
Nothing suggests a low glucose, and the flap explains the deficit.
The CT shows the flap entering the brachiocephalic trunk, which supplies the right carotid.
She has not had a seizure.

steps.x: **A. Carotid artery compromise by the dissection.** Type A + stroke = carotid involvement by the dissection.

questions.stem: A 76 year old man with a known 5.2 cm thoracic aortic aneurysm under surveillance collapses at home after sudden severe back pain. In the emergency department he is pale and clammy. His pulse rate is 106 bpm and BP 162/90 mmHg in the right arm and 128/74 mmHg in the left arm. Investigations: troponin I 12 ng/L (<34).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A pre-existing aortic aneurysm predisposes to dissection, which can present with back pain and collapse plus an arm BP difference.

steps.x: A diagnosis question: what does the known aneurysm predispose to?

clues: collapses at home after sudden severe back pain
162/90 mmHg in the right arm and 128/74 mmHg in the left arm
steps.x: Pre-existing **aneurysm** is a risk factor; back pain + collapse + **arm BP difference**.

elim: Biliary colic causes RUQ pain after meals, not collapse with a pulse deficit.
Troponin is normal and the arm difference points to the aorta.
Rupture follows vomiting and causes surgical emphysema.
PE does not give a 34 mmHg difference between arms.

steps.x: **A. Aortic dissection.** Aneurysm + sudden back pain + collapse + pulse deficit = dissection.

questions.stem: A 59 year old woman with hypertension attends the emergency department with sudden severe chest pain that was maximal at onset and radiates to her back. Her ECG shows sinus tachycardia only. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Aortic dissection is suspected.
questions.q: Which finding on examination would most support the suspected diagnosis?
o: Blood pressure difference over 20 mmHg between the arms
questions.e: A pulse deficit or BP difference greater than 20 mmHg between the arms is the key bedside sign of dissection.

steps.x: A finding question: which sign would you look for at the bedside?

clues: maximal at onset and radiates to her back
steps.x: Measure the BP in **both arms**: a difference **>20 mmHg** supports dissection.

elim: Points to DVT and pulmonary embolism.
Points to pericarditis.
Points to acute cholecystitis.
Points to musculoskeletal pain.

steps.x: **A. Blood pressure difference over 20 mmHg between the arms.** Dissection = check both arms; >20 mmHg difference is key.

questions.stem: A 48 year old man has sudden severe pain between his shoulder blades that began while straining at stool. It was at its worst immediately. His BP is 182/104 mmHg in the right arm and 180/102 mmHg in the left arm, and his femoral pulses are weak and delayed compared with the radial. His pulse rate is 98 bpm.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Sudden maximal interscapular pain with radio-femoral delay and equal arm pressures fits a type B dissection of the descending aorta.

steps.x: A diagnosis question that needs the subtype: use the pulses.

clues: 182/104 mmHg in the right arm and 180/102 mmHg in the left arm
femoral pulses are weak and delayed
steps.x: Equal arm pressures + **radio-femoral delay** = descending aorta = **type B**.

elim: ACS pain builds up and does not delay the femoral pulses.
Coarctation causes chronic radio-femoral delay, not sudden severe pain.
Equal arm pressures suggest the ascending aorta and arch branches are spared.
A disc does not alter femoral pulses.

steps.x: **D. Stanford type B aortic dissection.** Radio-femoral delay = type B; radio-radial delay = type A.

questions.stem: A 62 year old woman has sudden chest pain radiating to her back. She is haemodynamically stable with a pulse rate of 96 bpm and BP 164/90 mmHg in the right arm and 140/82 mmHg in the left arm. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm. A portable chest X-ray shows a widened mediastinum.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?
questions.e: In a stable patient the CT aortic angiogram is the gold standard, showing the false lumen and its extent.

steps.x: A diagnostic investigation question: is the patient stable enough for CT?

clues: 164/90 mmHg in the right arm and 140/82 mmHg in the left arm
steps.x: Stable, with a **widened mediastinum** and an arm difference: confirm with imaging of the whole aorta.

elim: Looks at the coronaries and could worsen a dissection; it will not show the false lumen.
Timed for the pulmonary arteries, not the aorta.
A widened mediastinum is suggestive but cannot confirm the diagnosis.
Cannot see the descending aorta well; CT is the gold standard in a stable patient.

steps.x: **B. CT aortic angiogram.** Stable suspected dissection = CT aortic angiogram.

questions.stem: A 71 year old man with hypertension has sudden tearing back pain. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 170/100 mmHg in the right arm and 146/88 mmHg in the left arm. He is stable and a CT aortic angiogram is performed to confirm the diagnosis.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on CT aortic angiogram?
o: A filling defect in the pulmonary artery
A fusiform aneurysm with mural thrombus
An intimal flap separating a true and a false lumen
questions.e: Blood entering the media through an intimal tear creates a false lumen, seen on CT as a flap dividing the aorta.

steps.x: A finding question on the gold-standard test.

clues: 170/100 mmHg in the right arm and 146/88 mmHg in the left arm
steps.x: This is a dissection: the CT shows the **false lumen**.

elim: That is pulmonary embolism.
That is an aneurysm without dissection.
That suggests a ruptured abdominal aneurysm.
That suggests constrictive pericarditis.

steps.x: **D. An intimal flap separating a true and a false lumen.** Dissection on CT = intimal flap with a false lumen.

questions.stem: A 55 year old man arrives in the emergency department with sudden severe chest pain radiating to between his shoulder blades. Bilateral arm blood pressures are being measured and a CT aortic angiogram has been requested. His pulse rate is 102 bpm and he is maintaining his blood pressure.
questions.q: Which blood tests are most appropriate as part of the first-line assessment?
questions.e: First-line bedside assessment is bilateral BPs with FBC and U&Es: haemoglobin for bleeding and renal function for contrast and renal involvement.

steps.x: A first-line investigation question: which bloods go with the bedside BPs?

clues: sudden severe chest pain radiating to between his shoulder blades
a CT aortic angiogram has been requested
steps.x: Bedside tests alongside the arm BPs: **FBC** (bleeding) and **U&Es** (kidneys, contrast).

elim: These look for pancreatitis, not part of the dissection work-up.
Not relevant to an acute aortic emergency.
Not relevant to acute chest pain management.
Not relevant to suspected dissection.

steps.x: **B. FBC and U&Es.** First-line in dissection: bilateral BPs, FBC, U&Es.

questions.stem: A 67 year old woman with suspected aortic dissection is intubated in resus after collapsing. Her pulse rate is 136 bpm and BP 72/44 mmHg despite fluids and vasopressors. The anaesthetist says she is too unstable to leave the department, and the cardiothoracic team needs to know if the ascending aorta is involved.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation?
questions.e: When the patient is too unstable for CT, transoesophageal echo at the bedside shows the flap and whether the ascending aorta is involved.

steps.x: An investigation question: CT is gold standard, but can she go to CT?

clues: BP 72/44 mmHg despite fluids and vasopressors
too unstable to leave the department
steps.x: **Unstable**, cannot travel: image at the bedside.

elim: Cannot see the ascending aorta.
Can show a wide mediastinum but cannot confirm or type a dissection.
The gold standard, but she is too unstable to be moved to the scanner.
Takes too long and needs transfer; unsuitable when unstable.

steps.x: **E. Transoesophageal echocardiography.** Unstable suspected dissection = TOE instead of CT.

questions.stem: A 60 year old man has sudden chest pain going through to his back. His ECG shows sinus rhythm with no ST changes. He is stable, with a pulse rate of 94 bpm and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His blood pressure is measured in both arms (see item resources).

visual.title: Systolic BP difference between arms
visual.label: Right 170, left 134
visual.caption: A difference over 20 mmHg is a key sign of dissection.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: An arm difference over 20 mmHg in a stable patient with chest pain to the back needs a CT aortic angiogram.

steps.x: A next-investigation question: read the visual first.

clues: chest pain going through to his back
blood pressure is measured in both arms
steps.x: The scale shows a **36 mmHg** difference: dissection until proved otherwise.

elim: Dangerous and irrelevant in a suspected dissection.
Would delay the diagnosis of a dissection.
Cannot exclude dissection of the descending aorta.
Looks for PE, not an aortic dissection.

steps.x: **A. CT aortic angiogram.** Arm BP difference >20 mmHg + stable = CT aortic angiogram.

questions.stem: A 54 year old man has a CT aortic angiogram showing a dissection flap arising in the ascending aorta. He has had IV morphine and an IV labetalol infusion. His pulse rate is now 62 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. There is no pericardial effusion. He has no major comorbidities.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Endovascular stent graft of the descending aorta
Immediate open surgery with aortic root replacement
questions.e: Type A dissection is always managed surgically: IV labetalol first, then immediate open surgery with aortic root replacement once diagnosed.

steps.x: A definitive management question: decide the Stanford type first.
Ascending aorta = **type A** = surgical emergency. BP has been controlled; now fix it.

elim: A type A dissection carries a high early mortality; delay is not acceptable.
Endovascular repair is for complicated type B, not the ascending aorta.
Thrombolysis would cause catastrophic bleeding.
Medical therapy alone is for stable type B.

steps.x: **C. Immediate open surgery with aortic root replacement.** Type A = labetalol, then immediate aortic root replacement.

questions.stem: A 69 year old woman has a CT aortic angiogram that shows a dissection limited to the descending thoracic aorta, distal to the left subclavian artery. Her limbs, kidneys and gut are well perfused. She has had IV morphine. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 178/100 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate drug to give now?
questions.e: Stable, uncomplicated type B is managed medically with IV beta-blockade (labetalol) to lower heart rate and BP and prevent propagation.

steps.x: A drug choice question in type B dissection.

clues: limited to the descending thoracic aorta
steps.x: Uncomplicated **type B** = medical. Rate and BP control first.

elim: Uncomplicated type B is managed medically; surgery is for complications.
A vasodilator alone causes reflex tachycardia, raising dP/dt; a beta-blocker comes first.
Too slow and does not lower heart rate.
Causes unpredictable falls in BP and reflex tachycardia.

steps.x: **C. IV labetalol.** Type B = IV labetalol and morphine; surgery only for complications.

questions.stem: A 73 year old man has an uncomplicated type B aortic dissection. He is on an IV labetalol infusion. He is in severe pain, scoring it 9/10, and is restless. His pulse rate is 88 bpm, BP 150/86 mmHg and respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute. His eGFR is 64 mL/min/1.73m².
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate analgesia?
questions.e: Opioid analgesia (IV morphine) controls pain, which also reduces the sympathetic drive that raises BP and heart rate.

steps.x: An analgesia question in a dissection.
Severe pain in dissection: **IV opioid**; pain control also helps BP control.

elim: NSAIDs are not adequate for this pain and risk renal and bleeding harm.
Entonox is short-acting and not used for ongoing dissection pain.
Too weak and too slow for severe dissection pain.
Not strong enough on its own.

steps.x: **C. IV morphine.** Dissection analgesia = IV morphine.

questions.stem: A 65 year old woman is on day 1 of medical treatment for a type B aortic dissection with IV labetalol and morphine. Her right leg becomes pale, cold and painful with absent femoral and foot pulses. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 128/76 mmHg. A repeat CT shows the false lumen compressing the right iliac artery.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
questions.e: Surgery (open or endovascular) is reserved for complicated type B dissection, such as malperfusion of a limb.

steps.x: A next step question: has the type B dissection become complicated?

clues: false lumen compressing the right iliac artery
steps.x: Type B with **malperfusion** is now complicated.

elim: Medical treatment alone is for uncomplicated type B; limb ischaemia is a complication.
She has a threatened limb.
Thrombolysis is contraindicated in dissection.
That is for chronic claudication.

steps.x: **E. Urgent surgical or endovascular repair.** Complicated type B (malperfusion) = intervention.

questions.stem: A 58 year old man with an uncomplicated type B aortic dissection has been started on IV labetalol and IV morphine in the emergency department. His pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 124/78 mmHg. He is comfortable. The medical registrar is deciding where he should be admitted.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate place for his ongoing care?
o: Coronary care unit with daily BP checks
Intensive care unit with continuous arterial BP monitoring
questions.e: All patients with aortic dissection need ICU care with continuous (arterial line) blood pressure monitoring while on IV therapy, as in ESC guidance.

steps.x: A setting-of-care question.
Even uncomplicated dissection needs **continuous** BP monitoring.

elim: Intermittent observations are not enough when BP must be tightly controlled.
Daily checks would miss changes in pressure.
He needs inpatient monitoring.
Ambulatory care is not appropriate for an aortic dissection.

steps.x: **D. Intensive care unit with continuous arterial BP monitoring.** Every dissection: ICU with continuous BP monitoring.

questions.stem: A 62 year old man has a confirmed type A aortic dissection. While waiting for theatre his BP falls to 80/50 mmHg and his pulse rate rises to 128 bpm. His JVP is raised and his heart sounds are muffled. Bedside echocardiography shows a pericardial effusion. The cardiothoracic surgeon is in the department.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Tamponade from a type A dissection is a surgical emergency: the definitive treatment is immediate open repair of the aortic root.

steps.x: A management question in a deteriorating type A dissection.
Type A with **tamponade**: get to theatre.

elim: Further beta-blockade would worsen shock.
Thrombolysis would worsen bleeding into the pericardium.
Diuresis would worsen tamponade by lowering filling.
He is in shock from a surgical emergency.

steps.x: **A. Emergency open surgical repair.** Type A + tamponade = emergency surgery.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman who is tall with arachnodactyly, joint hypermobility and an upward lens dislocation is found to have a dilated aortic root on echocardiography. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. She is counselled that she has an increased risk of aortic dissection.
questions.q: Which is the most likely defective protein?
questions.e: Marfan's syndrome is caused by defective fibrillin-1, which weakens the aortic media and predisposes to dissection.

steps.x: A science question: name the condition, then the protein.
Tall, arachnodactyly, **upward** lens dislocation, aortic root dilation = **Marfan's**.

elim: Defective in osteogenesis imperfecta.
Defective in vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, which does not cause lens dislocation.
Defective in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
Defective in supravalvular aortic stenosis (Williams syndrome).

steps.x: **E. Fibrillin-1.** Marfan's = fibrillin-1.

questions.stem: A 70 year old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension develops a type B aortic dissection. He has no features of a connective tissue disorder. His pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 188/104 mmHg. His registrar explains how his blood pressure has contributed.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism by which hypertension predisposes to dissection?
o: Spasm of the aortic smooth muscle
Weakening of the aortic media predisposing to an intimal tear
questions.e: Chronic hypertension weakens the aortic media, so the intima tears more easily and blood dissects into the wall.

steps.x: A mechanism question about a risk factor.

clues: no features of a connective tissue disorder
steps.x: Hypertension (like Marfan's) acts on the **media**.

elim: That is the mechanism of MI and arterial thrombosis.
That is the mechanism of embolic limb ischaemia.
That is syphilitic aortitis, not hypertension.
The aorta does not dissect through spasm.

steps.x: **E. Weakening of the aortic media predisposing to an intimal tear.** Hypertension and Marfan's weaken the media, which predisposes to intimal tears.

questions.stem: A 66 year old woman has a type B aortic dissection. Her CT aortic angiogram shows an entry tear in the intima just distal to the left subclavian artery, with blood flowing in a second channel alongside the true lumen. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 160/90 mmHg.
questions.q: Into which layer of the aortic wall has blood tracked to form the second channel?
o: Vessel lumen as an intraluminal thrombus
questions.e: Pulsatile blood passes through an intimal tear and dissects into the media, splitting it to create the false lumen.

steps.x: A pathophysiology question about the layers of the aortic wall.

clues: a second channel alongside the true lumen
steps.x: The tear is in the **intima**; the false lumen lies in the **media**.

elim: Blood here causes tamponade, not a second channel in the aorta.
Blood reaching the adventitia means rupture is imminent; the false lumen forms within the media.
The intima is the layer that tears, not where the false lumen forms.
A thrombus does not form a second flowing channel.

steps.x: **D. Tunica media.** Intimal tear + blood into the media = false lumen.

questions.stem: A 57 year old man with a type A aortic dissection is started on an IV labetalol infusion before transfer to theatre. The intensivist aims for a heart rate of about 60 bpm and a systolic BP of 100 to 120 mmHg. His pulse rate is currently 104 bpm and BP 166/94 mmHg.
questions.q: Which haemodynamic variable is most important to reduce to limit propagation of the dissection?
o: Rate of rise of aortic pressure (dP/dt)
questions.e: Beta-blockers lower heart rate and dP/dt, reducing shear stress on the aortic wall and limiting propagation, even before surgery in type A.

steps.x: A mechanism question about why beta-blockers are given.

elim: Lowering preload alone is not the aim and may cause reflex tachycardia.

questions.stem: A 61 year old woman has a type A aortic dissection involving the aortic root. A new early diastolic murmur is heard at the left sternal edge and her pulse pressure is wide. She has no history of rheumatic fever or valve disease, and her temperature is 36.8°C. Her pulse rate is 110 bpm and BP 158/48 mmHg.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of the murmur?
o: Calcific degeneration of the aortic valve
Distortion of the aortic valve annulus by the dissection
Rheumatic thickening of the valve cusps
questions.e: Aortic root involvement distorts the valve annulus so the cusps no longer meet: acute aortic regurgitation.
